headline: High-risk pair: shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict paths; nullclaw’s default logging/memory surfaces amplify compliance risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and editor buffers, while nullclaw exposes workspace files, webhooks, and MCP-like tool surfaces. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent writes attacker-controlled text into shared files or channels. The pathway is not proven by direct interaction evidence, so I choose medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace directory or synced files
IF nullclaw ingests file or webhook content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic instruction-following on file contents
Require provenance tags on shared artifacts
Review MCP/webhook inputs before execution
requires-engineering: add content-signed handoff channels

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers with broad network egress, and nullclaw touches conversation history, memory, audit logs, and secrets such as API keys and private keys. If they share files or credentials, either agent can expose sensitive material through its outbound calls. The default blast radius includes secrets and logs, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace files
IF either agent is given secrets or logs containing secrets
IF nullclaw forwards memory or webhook payloads to external services
mitigations: Use separate credential stores
Restrict shared folders to non-sensitive files
Rotate any exposed API keys
Disable outbound access for one agent during sensitive tasks
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. Continue shares state via filesystem, while nullclaw supports durable shared memory and modify_git_state. In a shared repo or workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide without locking, making destructive conflicts plausible by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git checkout
IF either agent writes generated code while the other edits the same files
IF nullclaw uses its durable memory to coordinate stale state
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories
Pause one agent during git operations
Use file locks around shared outputs
Review diffs before commit
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code changes and tool-driven outputs, and nullclaw has broader action surfaces including browser, webhook, schedule, and git. If nullclaw treats Continue’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into commits, messages, or scheduled actions. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF nullclaw consumes Continue output without independent verification
IF Continue-generated code or facts are used to trigger nullclaw actions
IF either agent is allowed to act on behalf of the user
mitigations: Require human review before actions
Add a verification step for all cross-agent outputs
Limit nullclaw to read-only mode for handoffs
Log source provenance on every transferred artifact
requires-engineering: implement typed, signed inter-agent contracts

E_compliance.rationale: Nullclaw explicitly touches audit logs, memory, webhook payloads, and secrets, while Continue touches workspace files and editor buffers. If regulated or personal data enters the shared workspace, nullclaw’s broader logging and network surfaces can create residency or retention mismatches. Continue is not cited separately because the compliance risk is driven mainly by nullclaw’s documented data handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace
IF audit logs or memory retain personal data longer than policy allows
IF webhook or API traffic crosses a restricted residency boundary
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Shorten log retention settings
Disable unnecessary webhooks
Review residency settings for external APIs
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls across both agents
